<reason>This was a tightly matched debate, but CON (A) ends with more live, un-neutralized ground. CON's persistent "who is the judge" pressure forced PRO to name a concrete standard (independent regulators using ghosting rates, time-to-match, complaint volume), and CON's counter that these are themselves "engagement metrics wearing a lab coat" (A4.2-4.3) exposed a real circularity in PRO's remedy that PRO never squarely answered in Rebuttal 2 or Closing. Similarly, CON's "renamed toll booth" critique of PRO's subscription-tier substitute (A4.5) — that paid filters/extra likes still buy preferential visibility — landed after PRO's own explanation of the substitute (B4.3) and was never rebutted, since B5 pivots back to the "engineered not to notice" framing instead. PRO's strongest recurring weapon, treating A2.6 ("ordered by prior engagement") as a flat concession, is rhetorically sharp but overstated: CON explicitly reframed it as an imperfect proxy rather than a corrupted signal (A4.1), so the "gotcha" doesn't fully land despite being repeated three times. PRO's closing rejoinder that "walking to Hinge" assumes transparency the motion denies, and that Hinge is Match-owned anyway, is a genuinely strong late counter-punch, keeping this close — but it arrives too late to recover the unanswered toll-booth and circularity points. CON's closing also does more explicit cost-weighing (mandate vs. choice, paywall vs. underserved users), giving the judge a cleaner decision calculus.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A4.2/A4.5 exchange (independent judge metrics are just "engagement metrics wearing a lab coat," and PRO's subscription-tier substitute is a "renamed toll booth") versus PRO's unanswered late counter that CON's "walk to Hinge" image assumes the very transparency the motion says these mechanics destroy (B5.3).</best_rebuttal>
